label: Lesson 1.1
title: What Is Scratch & Why Kids Love It

sections.heading: Why coding — and why now?
sections.text: Your child doesn't need to become a software engineer. But learning to code teaches something every kid can use: how to break a big problem into small steps , try an idea, see what happens, and fix it. That's problem-solving, creativity, and resilience rolled into one — and it happens to be fun. The hard part for most families isn't the child's interest. It's that the parent feels unqualified to help. This course removes that barrier. You don't need to know how to code today. You just need to stay one comfortable step ahead — and this lesson is that first step. You are not learning to be a programmer. You're learning to be a coding buddy — curious, encouraging, and just informed enough to help. 🌱 Growth mindset: the most important thing you'll teach isn't code Psychologists describe two ways people think about ability. A fixed mindset says, "I'm just not a computer person — you either have it or you don't." A growth mindset says, "I can't do this yet, but I can get better with practice." Research on learning keeps finding the same thing: the second belief is the one that helps people improve, because it turns every stumble into information instead of a verdict. Add the word "yet." "I don't understand loops" becomes "I don't understand loops yet ." One tiny word turns a dead end into a work in progress — for you and for your child. Plateaus are normal. Some sessions you'll feel like you're flying; others you'll feel stuck for a while. That flat stretch is usually your brain consolidating what it learned — not a sign you've hit your limit. It's a marathon, not a sprint. Twenty relaxed minutes a few times a week beats one exhausting three-hour cram. Nobody is timing you, and there's no test at the end. Why it matters for you: as an adult beginner, the inner voice saying "I'm too old / not techy enough for this" is the biggest obstacle you'll face — much bigger than any block. Why it matters for your child: kids learn how to handle frustration by watching the grown-ups beside them. When they see you hit a bug, shrug, and say "Hmm, it doesn't work yet — let's find out why," you're teaching the lesson that outlasts Scratch itself.

sections.heading: 🎓 Learn It: What Scratch actually is
sections.text: Scratch is a free website where kids make their own games, animations, and stories by snapping together colorful blocks instead of typing code. That's the whole idea in one sentence. It was created by the MIT Media Lab and is run by the non-profit Scratch Foundation. It's used by tens of millions of children around the world, in over 70 languages, and it's completely free. Figure 1: The Scratch editor. Kids drag blocks from the left into the middle to program the cat on the right. We'll tour every part in Lesson 1.2. 🧩 The three words that unlock Scratch Sprite — a character or object (the cat is a sprite). Stage — the screen where the action happens. Blocks — the instructions you snap together to make sprites do things. Learn these three and you can already follow along with your child.

sections.heading: 🎓 Learn It: Blocks vs. typing code
sections.text: "Real" coding usually means typing exact words and symbols. One wrong comma and nothing works — frustrating for adults, brutal for kids. Scratch throws that barrier away. Blocks only snap together if they make sense , so children can't create a "spelling mistake." They focus on ideas, not punctuation. Here's the same simple program in typed code and in Scratch blocks: Typed code (e.g. Python) when program starts: move(10) say("Hello!", 2) Miss a colon or misspell say and it breaks. The same thing in Scratch when ⚑ clicked move 10 steps say Hello! for 2 seconds Snaps together like LEGO. Nothing to misspell. Notice the colors. In Scratch, every block has a color that tells you its category — blue for movement, purple for looks, gold for events, and so on. Kids learn to "read" a program by its colors before they can read the words fluently. Motion Looks Sound Events Control Sensing Operators Variables ✅ Why this matters for your child Because blocks can't "break" from typos, kids get to the fun part — seeing their idea come alive — almost instantly. That quick reward is exactly what keeps them coming back.

sections.heading: 🎓 Learn It: Why kids love it
sections.text: Scratch is engineered around how children actually learn: by playing, tinkering, and showing off. Here's what makes it click:

label: Lesson 1.2
title: A Guided Tour of the Scratch Editor

sections.heading: 🎓 Learn It: Opening the editor
sections.text: Go to scratch.mit.edu and click “Create” at the top-left (or the big “Start Creating” button). That's it — the editor opens with the friendly orange cat waiting for you. You don't need an account to start playing. ✅ Account or no account? Without an account: you can build and test anything, but your project won't save automatically. Great for a first look. With a free account: projects save to the cloud and can be shared. We'll set one up safely at the end of this lesson.

sections.heading: 🎓 Learn It: The four areas (your map)
sections.text: The editor looks busy at first, but it's really just four zones . Learn these and you've learned the editor. Figure 1: The whole editor. Four zones — palette (left), code area (middle), stage (upper-right), sprite list (lower-right).

label: Lesson 1.3
title: Your First Project — Make the Cat Move & Talk

sections.heading: 🎬 What we're building
sections.text: Here's the finished program. Don't worry about how yet — this is our destination. When you click the green flag, the cat will walk to the right and greet you. when ⚑ clicked move 50 steps say Hello! I'm Scratch Cat for 2 seconds Three blocks. That's a complete, working program. Let's build it one block at a time. 💡 Before you start Open a fresh project at scratch.mit.edu → Create . Make sure the cat (Sprite1) is selected in the sprite list, so your blocks land on the cat.

sections.heading: 🎓 Learn It: Build it step by step
sections.text: Start with an Event Click the gold Events category. Drag “when 🟩 clicked” into the middle code area. This is the "hat" that starts your program. when ⚑ clicked Add some Motion Click the blue Motion category. Drag “move 10 steps” so it snaps underneath the hat block (you'll see a grey shadow when it's about to connect — let go there). when ⚑ clicked move 10 steps Now click the green flag. The cat scoots a tiny bit! Ten steps is small — we'll make it bigger soon. Make it talk Click the purple Looks category. Drag “say Hello! for 2 seconds” so it snaps below the move block. when ⚑ clicked move 10 steps say Hello! for 2 seconds Type your own words & a bigger move Click the white oval that says Hello! and type your own message, like Hello! I'm Scratch Cat . Then click the 10 in the move block and change it to 50 so the walk is easier to see. when ⚑ clicked move 50 steps say Hello! I'm Scratch Cat for 2 seconds ✅ That's it — you built a program! Click the green flag. The cat walks right and says hello. You just wrote software. 🎉

sections.heading: 🎓 Learn It: Run & understand it
sections.text: Click the green flag to run it; click the red stop to end it. Here's what happens, in order — this ordering is called a sequence , the most basic idea in all of coding:

sections.heading: 🎓 Learn It: What a sequence is
sections.text: A sequence is just a list of steps carried out one after another, top to bottom. You already built one in Module 1. Computers are wonderfully obedient and completely literal: they do exactly what you stack up, in exactly that order — no guessing what you meant. Think of a recipe: "crack the eggs, then whisk, then pour." Swap steps and breakfast goes sideways. Code is the same. A sequence is a recipe the computer follows to the letter. If it does something odd, it's usually following your recipe correctly — the recipe just isn't what you intended yet.

sections.heading: 🎓 Learn It: Order changes everything
sections.text: Here are two scripts with the same blocks in a different order . They behave completely differently: Move, then talk when ⚑ clicked move 100 steps say Made it! for 2 seconds Cat walks across, then speaks. Talk, then move when ⚑ clicked say Here I go! for 2 seconds move 100 steps Cat speaks first, then walks. ✅ Try the experiment Build one, run it, then drag the blocks to swap their order and run again. Feeling the difference is worth more than reading about it. 🌱 Growth mindset: the computer isn't judging you — it's giving you feedback When a script does something surprising, it's easy to think "I got it wrong." A more useful way to see it: the computer just showed you, very precisely, what your recipe actually says. That's free information. Swap two blocks, run it again, and compare — that loop of try, look, adjust is exactly how experienced coders work, too. Say it out loud when it happens to you: "Oh, interesting — it did what I told it, not what I meant. Let's fix the recipe." Your child will learn that a surprise is a clue to follow, not a reason to give up.

sections.heading: 🎓 Learn It: The wait block (your pacing tool)
sections.text: Computers are fast — often too fast. Without pauses, several actions blur into one instant. The “wait 1 seconds” block (from the orange Control category) is how you add breathing room, comic timing, and drama. Figure 1: The Control palette. The wait block is right at the top. Watch what a pause does to a knock-knock joke: when ⚑ clicked say Knock knock! for 2 seconds wait 1 seconds say Who's there? for 2 seconds wait 1 seconds say Boo! for 2 seconds Remove the waits and it still "works" — but the timing falls flat. Timing is where a project starts to feel alive .

sections.heading: 🛠️ Try It: Build a greeting routine
sections.text: Let's make the cat perform a little four-beat welcome. Open a fresh project and build this on the cat: Start with when 🟩 clicked (Events). Add go to x: 0 y: 0 (Motion) so it always starts centered. Add say “Hi, I'm Scratchy!” for 2 seconds (Looks). Add wait 1 seconds (Control). Add move 120 steps (Motion), then say “Welcome to my world!” for 2 seconds . when ⚑ clicked go to x: 0 y: 0 say Hi, I'm Scratchy! for 2 seconds wait 1 seconds move 120 steps say Welcome to my world! for 2 seconds 💡 Challenge: add a sound and a costume change Between the wait and the move, add start sound Meow (Sound) and next costume (Looks). Now it greets, meows, and its legs shift as it walks off. Six blocks, one little show.

sections.heading: 💬 Teach It: The "robot game"
sections.text: Sequences click into place fastest away from the screen, with a game kids adore: you become the robot. How to play Tell your child: "I'm a robot. I only do exactly what you say, one instruction at a time." Ask them to give you steps to, say, make a peanut-butter sandwich — and follow them literally . "Put peanut butter on the bread" → put the whole jar on the loaf. Let them laugh, then refine their instructions until it works. That's debugging a sequence! "Remember: the computer is a robot just like I was. It's not being silly on purpose — it's doing your steps exactly . So if it looks wrong, let's read our steps in order and find the mix-up." 👧 Ages 5–7 The robot game is the lesson. On screen, three blocks is plenty. Let them pick the words and the wait times. 🧒 Ages 8–11 Have them predict before pressing GO: "What happens first?" Prediction turns watching into thinking. 🧑 Ages 12+ Challenge them to time a two-sprite conversation using only waits. It's a great primer for loops next lesson. ⚠️ Common kid bug They put a say for 2 seconds before a move and wonder why the cat "waits." It's not stuck — that block holds for 2 seconds by design. Point out the words "for 2 seconds" and let the penny drop.

sections.heading: 🎯 Quick Check
sections.text: Question 1: What is a "sequence" in coding? Question 2: Which category holds the wait block? Question 3: Your child's cat "freezes" for two seconds mid-routine. Most likely reason?

sections.heading: 📓 Learning Journal
sections.text: Take five minutes to write it down Date a new entry, label it "Lesson 2.1," and give each prompt a line or two. Key concepts: Explain a sequence using a recipe or routine from your own day. Why does a computer follow it so literally? What clicked: When you swapped the order of the move and say blocks, what surprised you? Did the wait block change how the greeting felt? Questions & confusion: Anything about timing still puzzling — like why a "say … for 2 seconds" block already pauses on its own? Ideas to try: Write out a short scene (a joke, a greeting, a mini play) you could turn into a timed sequence next time. Progress & feelings: How did the robot game go? Who laughed first — you or your child? 💡 Teach It tip: Have your child write (or draw) the robot-game instructions in their coder's notebook as numbered steps. Then read them back and follow them exactly — spotting the missing step together is a perfect first taste of debugging.

sections.heading: Summary & What's Next
sections.text: 🎓 Key Takeaways A sequence runs top-to-bottom; order changes behavior. The wait block (Control) controls pacing and timing. Computers follow your steps literally — most "bugs" are a recipe mix-up. The off-screen "robot game" teaches sequencing better than any lecture. 🏅 What You've Accomplished Proved to yourself that block order changes behavior Used the wait block to pace a joke and a greeting Built a multi-step greeting routine from scratch Played the robot game to teach sequencing away from the screen 📋 Before the Next Lesson Save your greeting routine — we'll build on the cat's walk next time Let your child write their own knock-knock joke with waits Write your journal entry ❓ Common Questions at This Stage What's the difference between “say … for 2 seconds” and plain “say …”? “Say … for 2 seconds” shows the speech bubble, waits two seconds, removes it, and only then lets the next block run — so it acts like a built-in pause. Plain “say …” pops the bubble up and moves straight on, leaving it there until something else changes it. For step-by-step scenes, the “for … seconds” version is usually what you want. Can I use half a second or less in the wait block? Yes. Type any decimal, like 0.5 or 0.2 . Small waits are great for quick animations; longer ones (2–3 seconds) are good for giving a viewer time to read. My child thinks the robot game is "too babyish." Should I skip it? Flip the roles and raise the stakes: let them write the instructions for you , then follow them hilariously literally. Older kids love catching an adult "bug," and it teaches exactly the same idea. You can also skip straight to the screen — the Try It routine covers the concept too. 🔭 Looking Ahead Copy-pasting the same block ten times is nobody's idea of fun. In Lesson 2.2: Loops — Making Things Repeat we meet loops — the blocks that repeat actions for you — and finally make the cat truly walk. 💛 Encouragement for the Journey You've just learned the idea that sits under every program ever written: steps, in order. It may feel simple — that's because you understand it now. Everything ahead builds on this foundation.

sections.heading: 🎓 Learn It: Why loops exist
sections.text: Imagine you want the cat to take 20 little steps. You could drag in 20 "move" blocks. Painful — and if you wanted 21, you'd start over. A loop says "do this again and again" so one block replaces twenty. 😩 The hard way move 10 steps move 10 steps move 10 steps move 10 steps …and 16 more. No thanks. 😎 The loop way repeat 20 move 10 steps One loop. Change 20 to 100 in a heartbeat. Loops live in the orange Control category. Notice they're C-shaped — blocks you place inside the "mouth" of the C get repeated.

sections.heading: 🎓 Learn It: repeat vs. forever
sections.text: Figure 1: The two loops you'll use most — repeat and forever . Loop What it does Use it when… repeat 10 Runs the inside blocks a set number of times, then moves on You know how many times (blink 3 times, take 20 steps) forever Runs the inside blocks endlessly until you press stop Something should always be happening (a heartbeat, constant fall, always checking a key) ⚠️ "forever" never ends on its own Any block placed after a forever loop will never run — the program never gets past it. That's not a bug in Scratch; it's the loop doing its job. Use the red stop to end it.

sections.heading: 🎓 Learn It: What goes inside the loop
sections.text: This is the idea kids (and adults!) trip on: only the blocks inside the C repeat. Compare: Say is inside → repeats repeat 3 say Ha! for 1 seconds "Ha!" three times. Say is outside → runs once repeat 3 move 10 steps say Done! for 1 seconds Moves 3×, then says "Done!" once.

sections.heading: 🎓 Learn It: The if/then block
sections.text: An if/then block (orange Control category) says: " if something is true, then run the blocks inside." If it's not true, Scratch skips the inside and moves on. It's a fork in the road. if touching edge? then say Ouch! for 1 seconds The pointy hexagon slot only accepts a true/false question — called a condition . Those hexagon-shaped blocks come mostly from the Sensing category.

sections.heading: 🎓 Learn It: Sensing blocks
sections.text: Sensing blocks are the cat's "senses" — they answer questions about the world of your project. Figure 1: The Sensing palette. Hexagon blocks are true/false questions; ovals report values. Sensing block Answers… touching mouse-pointer? Is this sprite touching the pointer (or another sprite/edge)? key [space] pressed? Is that key being held down right now? mouse down? Is the mouse button being clicked? touching color? Is the sprite touching a specific color (great for mazes)? Drop a hexagon Sensing block into the hexagon slot of an if and you've built a sentence: " if touching the pointer, then …"

sections.heading: 🎓 Learn It: forever + if — the "game loop"
sections.text: Here's the pattern behind nearly every Scratch game: a forever loop that constantly checks an if . Because the check repeats endlessly, the sprite reacts the instant something becomes true. when ⚑ clicked forever if touching mouse-pointer? then start sound Meow Now whenever the mouse touches the cat, it meows — again and again — because the forever loop never stops asking. Without the forever, Scratch would check just once at the start and never again.

sections.heading: 🛠️ Try It: Set the scene
sections.text: Every story needs a place and a cast. Start a new project, then: Add a backdrop. Click the Choose a Backdrop button (bottom-right, below the stage panel) and pick a setting — say, "Forest." Add a second sprite. Click the Choose a Sprite cat button and pick a character to join the cat. The sprite library — hundreds of ready characters. The backdrop library — pick your setting. 💡 Remember from Lesson 1.2 Each sprite has its own code. Click a sprite in the sprite list before you add blocks, so the blocks land on the right character.

sections.heading: 🎓 Learn It: Positioning & glide
sections.text: The stage is a grid: x is left–right (−240 to 240), y is down–up (−180 to 180), and the center is x: 0, y: 0 . Two Motion blocks place your cast: go to x: __ y: __ — teleports instantly (use it to set a starting spot). glide 1 secs to x: __ y: __ — slides smoothly over time (lovely for entrances). when ⚑ clicked go to x: -200 y: -100 glide 2 secs to x: 0 y: -100 say Hello, forest! for 2 seconds Give the cat this script: it starts off-stage-left and glides to center as the story opens. Cinematic!

sections.heading: 🎓 Learn It: Broadcasts — the team signal
sections.text: Here's the problem: how does Sprite B know when Sprite A finished talking, so it can reply? Sprites can't see each other's scripts. The answer is a broadcast — a silent, invisible signal any sprite can shout, and any sprite can listen for. It's like a stage director calling "Cue: cat's done!" Every actor listening for that cue springs into action.

label: Lesson 3.2
title: A Simple Game with Variables & Score

sections.heading: 🎓 Learn It: What's a variable?
sections.text: A variable is a labeled box that holds a value the computer can remember and change — like a score, a life count, or a player's name. The box has a name ("score") and a value (0, then 1, then 2…). Think of a whiteboard on the wall labeled "SCORE." You can read what's on it, erase it, and write a new number. That's a variable. Variables live in the orange Variables category. The three blocks you'll use constantly: set [score] to 0 — put a specific value in the box change [score] by 1 — add to what's already there [score] (the reporter) — read the current value

sections.heading: 🎓 Learn It: Make a score variable
sections.text: Click the Variables category, then “Make a Variable.” Name it score , keep "For all sprites," and click OK. Figure 1: Making a variable. Name it clearly (like score ) and choose "For all sprites." Once created, a checkbox appears next to score in the palette — tick it and the score shows live on the stage. New blocks ( set , change , show/hide ) now use your variable.

sections.heading: 🗺️ The game plan
sections.text: Our game: apples fall from the top; move the cat with the mouse to catch them; each catch scores a point.

sections.heading: 🎓 Learn It: The debugging mindset
sections.text: Professional programmers spend more time fixing than writing. "Bug" is just the word for "not doing what I expected yet." The single most valuable thing you can model for your child is calm curiosity in the face of a bug. The computer isn't wrong and it isn't being mean. It's doing exactly what the blocks say. Debugging is the detective game of finding the gap between what you said and what you meant. ✅ Reframe the language Swap "It's broken / I failed" for "Interesting — let's find out why." Bugs become puzzles instead of defeats. This one habit protects a child's confidence for years. 🌱 Growth mindset: every bug is feedback, not a verdict A bug is the computer giving you precise, honest feedback: "here is exactly what your blocks told me to do." It isn't a judgment about whether you're a "computer person." Each one you track down teaches you something you'll never have to learn again — which is why experienced coders are mostly people who have made a lot of mistakes and paid attention to them. Let your child hear you say, "Ooh, a bug — what is it telling us?" When grown-ups treat mistakes as clues instead of failures, kids learn it's safe to try hard things.

sections.heading: 🎓 Learn It: The 4-step method
sections.text: When something's wrong, resist random flailing. Walk this loop instead:

sections.heading: 🎓 Learn It: Why one sprite isn't enough
sections.text: Remember the apple game from Lesson 3.2? One apple fell at a time. That works, but it's a bit lonely. What if you wanted twenty apples raining down at once? The obvious answer is to duplicate the apple sprite twenty times. Kids try this all the time, and it does work — right up until you want to change something. Make the apples fall faster, and now you're editing twenty sprites. Miss one and it behaves differently from the rest. Your sprite list becomes a mile long, and the project turns into a chore. Clones fix this. A clone is a copy of a sprite that Scratch makes while the program is running . You write the code once, in one sprite, and that sprite makes as many copies as it needs — then throws them away when they're done. Think of a rubber stamp . The stamp itself stays in your hand; you never see it on the paper. Each time you press it down, you get a print . Change the stamp, and every print after that changes too. In Scratch, the original sprite is the stamp, and clones are the prints.

sections.heading: 🎓 Learn It: The three clone blocks
sections.text: All three live at the very bottom of the orange Control category. Scroll down past the loops and if blocks and you'll find them. Figure 1: Scroll to the bottom of Control. “when I start as a clone” peeks in at the bottom; “create clone of myself” and “delete this clone” sit just below it. Block What it does Stamp analogy create clone of [myself] Makes a new copy of the sprite right now. The dropdown can also clone a different sprite. Press the stamp down when I start as a clone A hat block. Only a brand-new clone runs the script under it — the original never does. What each print does after it lands delete this clone Removes the clone that runs it. (Nothing happens if the original runs it.) Wipe the print away The original (the stamp) when ⚑ clicked hide forever create clone of myself wait 1 seconds Each clone (the prints) when I start as a clone show say I'm a copy! for 2 seconds delete this clone This two-script shape is the pattern you'll use for almost every clone project: the original hides and makes clones in a forever loop with a wait ; each clone shows itself, does its job, and deletes itself. The wait matters — without it, the loop would make clones as fast as the computer can go and hit the limit in a split second.

label: Lesson 4.2
title: My Blocks — Make Your Own Blocks

sections.heading: 🎓 Learn It: Why make your own blocks?
sections.text: By now your projects are getting bigger. You've probably noticed that scripts grow long, and that the same little group of blocks shows up again and again: a jump here, the same jump there, another copy for when the cat touches something. Long, repetitive scripts are hard to read, and when you want to change the jump you have to hunt down every copy. Think of a recipe card that says "Make pancakes." Those two words stand for a whole list of steps: crack the eggs, whisk, pour, flip. Once the card is written, you just say "make pancakes" and everybody knows what to do. A custom block works the same way. You write the steps once , give them a name, and from then on one block stands for all of them. It's like teaching a dog a new trick: you practice the steps together, then you only have to say "roll over." Programmers call a named chunk of code a function (or sometimes a procedure ). You don't need to use those words with your child, but it's nice to know that when you make a block in Scratch, you're doing exactly what professional coders do in Python or JavaScript every day.

label: Lesson 4.3
title: Capstone — Plan & Build a Game Together

sections.heading: 🎬 What we're building
sections.text: Star Catcher works like this. Stars fall from random spots at the top of the screen. You slide a bowl left and right with the arrow keys. Each star you catch adds a point to your score . Each star that hits the ground costs you one of your three lives . When the lives run out, a big GAME OVER appears and everything stops. Here's where each thing you've learned shows up: Game piece Idea it uses Where you learned it Bowl moves with arrow keys forever + if + key pressed Lesson 2.3 Score and lives Variables Lesson 3.2 Lots of falling stars Clones Lesson 4.1 One block that resets the game My Blocks Lesson 4.2 Game Over appears Broadcasts Lesson 3.1 But the most important skill in this lesson isn't a block at all. It's planning . That comes first.

sections.heading: 🎓 Learn It: Plan before you code
sections.text: When kids start a game by opening Scratch and dragging blocks, it usually ends in one of two ways. Either the game gets too big to finish, or nobody is quite sure what it's supposed to do. Five minutes of planning on paper prevents both. Here's the routine: Brainstorm. Toss out lots of game ideas with no judging. Silly ones are welcome ("a taco that dodges forks!"). Pick ONE small idea. Choose something with one main action: catch, dodge, jump, or chase. Save the other ideas on a "someday" list so nobody feels their idea was thrown away. Sketch it on paper. Draw the stage. Where does the player start? What moves? How do you score? How do you win or lose? List the pieces as a checklist. Every sprite, every variable, every rule becomes a line you can tick off. That list is your to-do list. Build the smallest playable version first. Get the core action working, even if it's plain. Then add one thing, test it, and add the next. That last step is a loop that professional game studios use too:

label: Lesson 5.1
title: The Art of Not Taking Over

sections.heading: Why "not taking over" matters
sections.text: When we grab the mouse and fix the bug, we get a working project — and rob our child of the exact moment learning happens. The struggle is the lesson. Your goal isn't a polished project; it's a child who believes "I can figure things out." Every time you solve it for them, you quietly teach: "this is too hard for you." Every time you help them solve it themselves, you teach: "you are a person who solves hard things."

sections.heading: 🎓 Scaffolding: help that fades
sections.text: Scaffolding means giving just enough support to keep your child moving, then removing it bit by bit as they gain confidence — like training wheels you gradually raise. Aim to give the least help that unblocks them.

sections.heading: 🎓 Accounts & privacy
sections.text: Scratch is run by a non-profit and takes children's privacy seriously (it complies with children's privacy laws like COPPA in the US). When your child signs up, Scratch asks for a parent/guardian email and collects minimal information. Figure 1: The official Scratch for Parents page — your best reference for privacy and safety specifics, straight from the source. ✅ Set up the account the safe way Use a username that hides real identity (no full name, school, or birth year). Enter your email as the parent contact — you'll get account notices. Choose a password together and keep it somewhere you both can find it. Remind them: never share real name, address, school, phone, or photos in projects or comments.

sections.heading: 🎓 Private by default
sections.text: A crucial reassurance: projects are NOT public until your child explicitly clicks “Share.” Everything they build stays private to their account until then. Nothing is broadcast to the world by accident.

sections.heading: 🎬 Meet ScratchJr
sections.text: ScratchJr is a free app made for children about 5 to 7 years old. It runs on iPads, Android tablets, and Chromebooks. Like Scratch, kids snap blocks together to make characters move, talk, and play sounds. The difference is that every block is a picture , so a child who can't read yet can still code. Figure 1: The ScratchJr website, where you'll find download links plus guides for parents and teachers. By the end of this lesson you'll have built this: tap the pet, and it hops, grows, and says hello in your child's own recorded voice . 👆 Start on Tap ⤴️ Hop 2 🔼 Grow 2 🎙️ My Sound 🔽 Shrink 2 ⏹️ End 💡 Before you start Install ScratchJr from your tablet's app store (search “ScratchJr”; it's free, with no ads or in-app purchases). Open it, tap the house icon, then tap the big + to start a new project. A cat appears on the stage, just like in Scratch.

sections.heading: 🎓 Learn It: How ScratchJr differs from Scratch
sections.text: Because you know Scratch, ScratchJr will feel familiar. The big ideas carry over: events start scripts, blocks run in order, loops repeat. What changes is everything that would trip up a small child. Scratch ScratchJr Block direction Blocks stack top to bottom Blocks snap side by side in a row, read left to right like a sentence Reading Every block has words Blocks show pictures ; only a few, like “Say,” take typed words Number of blocks Well over a hundred Only a few dozen, so there's less to hunt through Device Computer web browser (or the desktop app) Made for tablets : tap and drag with a finger Sharing Online community, projects on the web Projects stay on the device , with no public community Numbers “Steps” (tiny units) Grid squares, so a child can count moves on a visible grid That last row about sharing is a quiet gift for parents. There are no comments, followers, or strangers to worry about. Projects live in the app on that tablet. Some versions let you send a copy by email or AirDrop, but there's no public website to post to. (The community safety habits from Lesson 5.2 can wait until your child moves up to Scratch.)

sections.heading: 🎓 Learn It: Six colors of picture blocks
sections.text: Tap a colored button on the left of the block area and that category's blocks slide into view. Color tells you what a block does, just like in Scratch, though some of the colors don't match the ones you already know: 🟡 Triggering 🔵 Motion 🟣 Looks 🟢 Sound 🟠 Control 🔴 End Color What it does Blocks you'll use most 🟡 Triggering Starts a script, like Scratch's Events Start on Green Flag, Start on Tap (tapping the character), Start on Bump (touching another character), Start on Message 🔵 Motion Moves the character around the stage Move right/left/up/down, Turn, Hop, Go Home 🟣 Looks Changes how it looks Say (a speech bubble), Grow, Shrink, Reset Size, Hide, Show 🟢 Sound Makes noise Pop, plus any sounds you record with the microphone 🟠 Control Changes timing and repetition Wait, Stop, Set Speed, Repeat (wraps around other blocks) 🔴 End Caps the end of a script End, Repeat Forever, Go to Page Many blocks have a small number under them. For Motion blocks, that number counts grid squares . Tap the grid button above the stage to show the grid, and “Move right 3” becomes something a child can count with a finger: one, two, three squares. 🎨 Watch out: the colors don't match Scratch In Scratch, green is Operators and sound is pink. In ScratchJr, green is Sound and yellow starts things. That doesn't bother kids at all, but it can confuse you if you're switching between the two apps. Trust the pictures.

sections.heading: 🛠️ Try It: “My Pet Says Hi”
sections.text: Build this yourself first (it takes about ten minutes) so you know where everything is before you sit down with your child. Pick or make a pet Tap the + beside the character list to open the library and choose an animal. Or tap the paintbrush to open the paint editor and draw one. The paint editor also has a camera tool: tap it, tap inside a shape, and take a photo, and the photo fills that shape. Kids love putting their own face on a character. Start on tap Tap the yellow button and drag Start on Tap (a finger touching a character) into the script area. Now the script will run whenever someone taps the pet. Hop and grow From blue , drag Hop so it snaps onto the right side of the trigger. From purple , snap Grow on after it. Tap the pet on the stage to test it. 👆 Start on Tap ⤴️ Hop 2 🔼 Grow 2 Record a sound Tap green , then the microphone block. Press record, say “Hi! I'm your pet!” (or bark, or giggle), stop, and accept it. A new sound block appears. Snap it on after Grow. Shrink back and end Add a purple Shrink so the pet returns to normal size (otherwise it keeps growing with every tap), then cap the row with the red End block. 👆 Start on Tap ⤴️ Hop 2 🔼 Grow 2 🎙️ My Sound 🔽 Shrink 2 ⏹️ End ✅ Tap the pet! It hops, puffs up, says hi in a real voice, and settles back down. That's a complete program with an event, a sequence, and a sound. It's the same thinking as your first Scratch cat, laid out sideways.

sections.heading: 🛠️ Try It: A two-page story
sections.text: ScratchJr projects can have up to four pages , like pages in a picture book. Each page has its own background and characters. Let's make the pet invite us somewhere new. Add page 2 Tap the + in the page strip on the right side of the screen. A blank page 2 appears. Tap the background button to pick a scene (a park, a bedroom, outer space) and add a character. On page 1, turn the page Go back to page 1. Give the pet a second script that starts with the green flag, says something, then ends with Go to Page . Once a second page exists, the red End category shows a Go to Page block with a little picture of that page. 🏁 Start on Green Flag 💬 Say Come to my house! ⏱️ Wait 10 📄 Go to Page 2 On page 2, say hello On page 2, give its character a green-flag script too. When the story turns to a new page, that page's green-flag scripts start up. 🏁 Start on Green Flag ➡️ Move Right 3 💬 Say Welcome home! ⏹️ End Press the green flag above the stage (or use the full-screen button to present it) and watch the story play across two pages. The pet from Try It 1 still responds to taps on page 1, too.

sections.heading: 🐛 Common problems & fixes
sections.text: What you see Likely cause Fix Tapping the pet does nothing The script starts with Green Flag, or a block isn't snapped on Use Start on Tap ; drag blocks until they click together in one row The pet gets bigger and bigger Grow with no Shrink or Reset Size Add Shrink (same number) or Reset Size at the end The pet walks off the stage Moves add up each run Add the blue Go Home block at the start of the row Recording is silent The app doesn't have microphone permission Allow the microphone in the tablet's settings for ScratchJr Page 2 never appears No Go to Page block, or the script before it never runs Check page 1's row ends with Go to Page and starts with a trigger that actually fires A block “vanished” It was dragged back onto the block palette, which deletes it Drag a fresh one out; no harm done 🌱 Growth mindset: wobbly is what learning looks like Nobody rides a bike smoothly the first time. The wobbling is the learning. Your five-year-old will drop blocks in the wrong spot and make a pet that grows until it fills the screen, and you may find sideways rows odd after weeks of Scratch. That's experimenting, not failing. When a script flops, laugh and say, “Whoa, that's not what we planned! What should we try?” A child who hears that at five learns that surprises are interesting instead of scary.

sections.heading: 💬 Teach It: Coding with a very young child
sections.text: Coaching a five-year-old is different from coaching an older child. Their attention comes in short bursts, their fingers are still learning to drag, and their imagination is huge. Plan around all three. Keep sessions short: 10–15 minutes Stop while it's still fun, ideally right after a big laugh. Ending on a high means they'll ask to do it again tomorrow. Two short sessions a week will get you further than one long, tearful one. Tell the story first, then code it Before touching the tablet, ask for a tiny story out loud: who is in it and what happens . Then turn each thing that happens into a block. “So the puppy jumps, gets really big, and barks. Which picture looks like jumping? …Yes, the hop! What comes next in your story?” You read, they tap If there's anything to read, like a menu or a Say bubble, you read it aloud. They tap, drag, and press the green flag. Keep your hands in your lap. If a drag keeps missing, steady the tablet rather than doing it for them. Let them record silly sounds The microphone is the most motivating feature in the whole app. Burps, animal noises, a sibling's name, “I'm a dinosaur!”: let them record whatever they like. Hearing their own voice come out of a character they coded is pure magic. Celebrate out loud “You made the puppy do that! You told it what to do, and it listened. That's what coders do.” 👶 Ages 4–5 Sit them on your lap and treat it as a shared picture book. You set up the character; they choose the blocks from two or three you point to and do all the tapping. One trigger plus two or three blocks is plenty. Recording sounds is the whole show. 👧 Ages 5–6 They drag and snap on their own while you sit beside them. Build “My Pet Says Hi” together, then invite changes: “What else could it do when you tap it?” Introduce the grid by counting squares together for Move blocks. 🧒 Ages 6–7 Give a goal, not steps: “Make a story with two pages.” Let them draw characters, snap in their own photo, and try Repeat or Start on Bump. Ask them to explain their row to you, left to right, like reading a sentence. 🌟 End with a show Use full-screen mode and have them “perform” their story for the family, tapping the pet on cue. Clapping and asking for an encore beats any sticker chart.

sections.heading: 🎓 When to move up to Scratch
sections.text: There's no graduation date. Most kids are ready to try full Scratch at around 7 or 8 , but readiness matters more than age. Look for these signs: Reading comfort. They can sound out short block labels like “move 10 steps” without getting frustrated. They want more. They ask for things ScratchJr can't do, like keeping score or making a game with rules. They're outgrowing four pages. Their stories keep bumping into the limits. They can use a mouse or trackpad , since Scratch is mostly built for a computer. You don't have to switch all at once. Many kids happily use both for a while. When you do move over, point out what carries across: “Remember the yellow start blocks? In Scratch they're called Events. And instead of a row, the blocks stack up like a tower.” Then begin with Lesson 1.3 's moving, talking cat, which is the same idea as their pet.

sections.heading: 🎯 Quick Check
sections.text: Question 1: How are blocks arranged in a ScratchJr script? Question 2: You want the pet to react when your child touches it on the screen. Which block starts the script? Question 3: What's the best length for a ScratchJr session with a 5-year-old?

sections.heading: 📓 Learning Journal
sections.text: Take five minutes to write it down A notebook, a notes app, or a sticky note on the fridge all work. Writing it down helps it stick, and your notes will help you plan the next session with your little one. Key concepts: In your own words, how is a ScratchJr row like a Scratch stack, and how is it different? Which of the six block colors would your child use most? What clicked: Was there a moment when ScratchJr made a coding idea feel simpler, like counting grid squares or hearing a recorded voice come out of a character? Questions & confusion: Did anything trip you up, such as the mismatched colors, pages, or finding the microphone? Write it down so you can check it before your child sits down. Ideas to try: Jot down one tiny story your child could turn into a two-page ScratchJr project. Who's in it, and what happens? Progress & feelings: How did it feel to hand the tablet to a very young child and keep your hands in your lap? What made them laugh? 💡 Teach It tip: Young kids can journal too. Ask them to draw their pet and what it did, and write their words underneath for them. Months later, those drawings are a wonderful record of how they grew.

sections.heading: Summary
sections.text: 🎓 Key Takeaways ScratchJr is a free tablet app (iPad, Android, Chromebook) for ages 5–7 that uses picture blocks, so no reading is needed. Blocks snap into a horizontal row read left to right, in six colors: yellow Triggering, blue Motion, purple Looks, green Sound, orange Control, and red End. Projects can have up to four pages , and Go to Page turns them like a picture book. Projects stay on the device, with no public community. Coach little ones in 10–15-minute sessions: story first, you read, they tap, lots of silly sounds and celebration. Move up to Scratch at around 7–8 , when reading is comfortable and they want more than ScratchJr offers. 🏅 What You've Accomplished Learned a second coding tool in a single sitting Built a tap-to-talk pet with a recorded sound Made a two-page story with Go to Page Planned a coaching style that fits a very young child 📋 Before the Next Lesson Install ScratchJr on a tablet your child can use Do one 10-minute “My Pet Says Hi” session together Browse the guides for parents on scratchjr.org Write your journal entry ❓ Common Questions at This Stage My child is 4. Is that too young for ScratchJr? Not if you're sitting together. ScratchJr is designed for 5–7, but plenty of 4-year-olds enjoy it on a parent's lap. Keep it very short, focus on tapping and recording sounds, and don't worry about “finishing” anything. If it isn't fun yet, put it away for a few months and try again. We don't have a tablet. Can we use ScratchJr on a laptop? ScratchJr is built for tablets and Chromebooks. If you only have a regular computer, you can still use full Scratch with a young child. Just follow the Ages 5–7 coaching tips in each lesson: you read and drag if needed, and they choose and press the green flag. My 6-year-old has an older sibling on Scratch and wants to use that instead. Should I say no? No need. Let them try Scratch next to their sibling; if it frustrates them, offer ScratchJr as “your own coding app.” Kids often move back and forth. The concepts are the same, so time in either one counts. 🔭 Looking Ahead In the course finale, Lesson 5.4: What Comes After Scratch , you'll map the whole road ahead: going deeper in Scratch, coding that controls real-world gadgets, and the gentle bridge from blocks to typed languages like Python. Whether your child is 5 or 15, you'll leave knowing their next step. 💛 Encouragement for the Journey You didn't just learn to code this course. You learned to make coding fit a child, even one who can't read yet. That flexibility is the heart of great teaching, and your little one is lucky to have you as their first coding buddy. 🏠 Back to Course Home
